title: Wave quantities and phase

learning_outcomes.text: understand and use the terms displacement, amplitude, phase difference, period, frequency, wavelength and speed

prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy from place to place.
The disturbance travels while a medium element oscillates locally about equilibrium.
AS Topic 1 quantities, units, scalars and vectors.
new_learning: Displacement records position relative to equilibrium and includes direction.
Phase compares the stages of oscillation of two points or two moments.

blocks.heading: The same wave, six different measurements
content: A row of floating markers rises and falls as a ripple passes. At one instant, one marker is highest, another is crossing its resting level, and a third is lowest. How can all three belong to the same repeating wave but be at different stages?
We need a precise language for where a point is, how far it moves, how quickly the motion repeats, how far the pattern repeats and how the stages compare.

figure.purpose: Create the need for position, repeat and phase quantities.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of five floating markers on one ripple profile at different stages. Mark only an equilibrium line and letters P to T, without quantity labels that answer later prompts.
figure.alt_text: Five labelled floating markers occupy different positions on a repeating ripple above and below equilibrium.

blocks.heading: Position now: displacement and amplitude
content: Displacement tells us where one particle or point on the wave is relative to its equilibrium position at a chosen instant. Choose one side of equilibrium as positive. A point on the other side has negative displacement. Displacement can change continuously as the point oscillates.

Definition to learn: amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position. Amplitude is a positive size. It is measured from equilibrium to one extreme, not from the lowest point to the highest point.
For example, if a bead ranges from +3.0 cm to -3.0 cm, its amplitude is 3.0 cm. Its peak-to-peak distance is 6.0 cm, which is not its amplitude.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position

figure.purpose: Distinguish signed displacement, amplitude and peak-to-peak distance.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated vertical scale beside an oscillating bead. Show equilibrium, +3.0 cm and -3.0 cm, one instantaneous displacement arrow, an amplitude bracket and a separate crossed-out peak-to-peak amplitude claim.
figure.alt_text: An oscillating bead diagram distinguishes instantaneous signed displacement, 3.0 cm amplitude and 6.0 cm peak-to-peak distance.

blocks.heading: Repeating in time: period and frequency
content: Definition to learn: period is the time taken for one complete oscillation or wave cycle. Its symbol is T and its SI unit is the second, s.
Definition to learn: frequency is the number of complete oscillations or wave cycles per unit time. Its symbol is f and its SI unit is the hertz, Hz. One hertz means one complete cycle per second.
Formula to remember: T = 1/f. Period and frequency describe the same repetition from opposite viewpoints. A shorter time for each cycle means more cycles each second. The rearranged form is f = 1/T.

controlled_definitions.accepted_definition: the time taken for one complete oscillation or wave cycle
the number of complete oscillations or wave cycles per unit time

figure.purpose: Connect one-cycle time with cycles-per-second counting.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-panel sequence. Left brackets one complete cycle on a displacement-time trace as T. Right counts four complete cycles inside one second as 4 Hz. Add T equals 1 over f below.
figure.alt_text: A time trace shows one period, while a second panel counts complete cycles per second to show frequency.

blocks.heading: Count a reliable time interval
content: A marker completes five full oscillations in 2.0 s. Start by checking that the count is of complete cycles, not turning points. The period is the time per cycle: T = 2.0 s / 5 = 0.40 s.
Now use the formula to remember. Since f = 1/T, f = 1 / 0.40 s = 2.5 Hz. The unit says the marker completes 2.5 cycles each second.
Independent check: 2.5 cycles per second for 2.0 s gives 5.0 cycles, matching the observation. Counting several cycles reduces the effect of a small timing uncertainty.

figure.purpose: Model a complete period-frequency calculation with units and a reverse check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout with five hand-drawn cycles spanning 2.0 s, followed by T equals 2.0 divided by 5 and f equals 1 divided by 0.40, then a small reverse-check box.
figure.alt_text: Five cycles in 2.0 seconds lead to a period of 0.40 seconds and frequency of 2.5 hertz, with a reverse check.

blocks.heading: Repeating in space: wavelength
content: Definition to learn: wavelength is the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase. Its symbol is λ and its SI unit is the metre, m.

On one snapshot of a repeating wave, adjacent crests are in phase, so their separation is one wavelength. Adjacent troughs also work. A crest and the next trough are not one wavelength apart because they are at different stages.

Time and space answer different questions. Period is the shortest repeat time at one point. Wavelength is the shortest repeat distance across the wave at one instant. Wave speed describes how quickly the disturbance advances, but its equation is saved for the next module.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase

figure.purpose: Contrast correct same-phase wavelength measurements with a tempting half-cycle distance.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper wave snapshot with brackets between adjacent crests and adjacent troughs labelled lambda. Also show a crest-to-trough bracket labelled half a wavelength, not wavelength.
figure.alt_text: A wave snapshot identifies one wavelength between adjacent crests or troughs and half a wavelength from crest to trough.

blocks.heading: Phase is a stage, not just a height
content: It can feel natural to say that two points with the same displacement are in phase. That is sometimes true, but equal height alone is not enough. One point may be moving upward while the other is moving downward.

Two points are in phase when they are at the same stage of their cycle, so they have the same displacement and the same direction of motion. Adjacent crests are in phase. A crest and a trough differ by half a cycle, so their phase difference is 180°. A quarter-cycle separation corresponds to 90°.

One full cycle is 360°. For a spatial separation Δx on a wave of wavelength λ, the phase difference is the fraction Δx/λ of 360°. The same idea works in time using Δt/T. These fraction-of-a-cycle relationships express phase; they are not new wave-speed equations.

figure.purpose: Repair the misconception that equal displacement alone proves equal phase.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison of four labelled points on a sinusoidal trace. Pair two equal positive displacements with opposite motion arrows and mark not in phase. Pair two adjacent crests and mark in phase. Include a small cycle wheel for 90, 180 and 360 degrees.
figure.alt_text: Equal-height points moving in opposite directions are contrasted with adjacent crests at the same stage of their cycle.

blocks.heading: Choose the quantity that matches the question
content: Use displacement for a point's signed position now and amplitude for its greatest displacement from equilibrium. Use period for seconds per cycle and frequency for cycles per second. Use wavelength for the shortest spatial repeat between adjacent in-phase points. Use phase difference to compare stages of oscillation.

A quick representation check prevents common errors. A displacement-time graph follows one place through time, so horizontal repeats give period. A displacement-distance snapshot compares places at one instant, so horizontal repeats give wavelength.

Carry the Lesson 1 model with you: the measured point oscillates locally while the progressive disturbance and energy travel onward. These quantities describe that motion precisely without yet using the wave equation or CRO controls.

figure.purpose: Summarise the choice among displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, wavelength and phase.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map beginning with position now, largest displacement, repeat in time, repeat in space and compare stages. Connect each prompt to the correct quantity, symbol and unit where applicable.
figure.alt_text: A decision map links common measurement questions to displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, wavelength and phase difference.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

concepts_taught: wave speed as the rate of advance of a disturbance without its equation
misconceptions_addressed: Equal displacement alone means points are in phase.
Period and wavelength are read from the same horizontal axis.
next_lesson_can_assume: Distinguish displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, wavelength and wave speed in words.
Use T = 1/f with seconds and hertz.
Read period from a time representation and wavelength from a spatial representation.
Express phase difference as a fraction of a cycle and in degrees.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Use CRO y-gain or time-base controls.
